title: JavaScript Modules: From require() to import() — The Complete Notes
summary: A dense field guide to JavaScript's module systems: how CommonJS and ES modules actually load, link, and cache, every import/export form, surviving circular imports and dynamic import(), and what bundlers and package.json really do to your module graph.

chapters.title: Modules 101: The Problem & the Two Systems
points: Definition: a module is a file with its own scope — nothing leaks; values are shared only via explicit export/import
Problems modules solve: global name collisions, implicit load-order dependencies, untestable coupling
Pre-2015 workaround: IIFEs and the revealing module pattern — privacy by function scope, but no dependency graph
CommonJS (2009, Node): require() / module.exports — synchronous, built for local disk and servers
ES Modules (ES2015): import / export — static graph parsed before code runs, built for browsers and async networks
Legacy systems you'll still meet: AMD (RequireJS) and UMD shims — bridging formats from the pre-ESM browser era
Script vs module: module code is always strict mode, and top-level this is undefined
A file only becomes a module when loaded as one: type="module", .mjs, or package.json "type":"module" — same syntax, different world
Modules are singletons: first import evaluates the file, every later import receives the cached instance
Live bindings preview: ESM importers see a read-only view of the exporter's variables, not copied values (details in ch. 5)
Timeline gotcha: ESM was standardized in 2015 but Node only stabilized it around v12 (2019) — why half the ecosystem still ships CJS
Mental model: a program is a dependency graph of files; import/export are just the edges

chapters.title: CommonJS Mechanics: require() Under the Hood
points: require('./x') resolves, loads, evaluates the file, and returns its module.exports — synchronously, blocking until done
Resolution order: core modules → relative/absolute paths → walk up parent directories into node_modules
Path resolution details: tries .js / .json / .node extensions, then folder/index.js — silent defaults you must know
Node wraps every file in function(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) { ... } — that's where those 'globals' come from
exports is an alias for module.exports: reassigning exports = {} breaks the link — set module.exports for a single big export
require.cache is keyed by resolved filename; a body runs once — delete require.cache[id] to force re-evaluation (tests use this)
It's just a function call: require() works inside if-branches, loops, or with computed strings — a dynamic, runtime graph
Lazy-loading pattern: put require() inside functions to defer heavy dependencies until first call
require('./data.json') auto-parses JSON into an object — free config loading
Circular imports in CJS: the cycle returns a partially filled exports object (full treatment in ch. 6)
Bundler pain: dynamic require(variable) can't be statically traced — bundlers bail or need context/glob plugins

chapters.title: ESM Exports: Every Form
points: Inline named exports: export const x = 1; export function f() {} — the everyday case
Export list at the bottom: export { a, b as betterName } — one glanceable API surface, renaming via as
Default export: export default expression — one per module; importers name it whatever they like
Under the hood, default is a named export literally called "default" — that's why namespaces expose it as .default
export default accepts anonymous functions/classes or any expression, even an object literal
Re-export: export { x } from './m.js' — forwards the binding without creating a local one
Re-exporting defaults: export { default } from './m.js' and export { default as X } from — barrel-file staples
export * from './m.js' re-exports everything except default; name collisions between star re-exports are silently skipped
export * as ns from './m.js' (ES2020): expose a whole submodule under one name
Exports are static declarations: top level only — no export inside if, loops, or functions
Exported bindings can't be reassigned by importers — they are read-only live views (mechanics in ch. 5)

chapters.title: ESM Imports: Every Form
points: Named import: import { a, b as alias } from './m.js' — brace names must match exports exactly; alias with as
Default import: import anything from './m.js' — your name, their default; mix both: import React, { useState } from 'react'
Namespace import: import * as utils from './m.js' — a frozen, read-only module namespace object
Side-effect import: import './polyfills.js' — runs the module for its effects, binds nothing
Specifier kinds: relative './x.js', absolute '/x.js', bare 'lodash' (resolved via node_modules), full URLs in browsers
Unlike require(), Node ESM needs explicit extensions ('./utils.js', not './utils') — the #1 migration error
All static imports are hoisted: dependencies evaluate before the importing module's body, depth-first, in specifier order
import.meta.url — the module's own URL; the ESM replacement for __dirname/__filename (recipes in ch. 9)
Import attributes: import data from './data.json' with { type: 'json' } — required for non-JS types; replaces the old assert keyword
Imports are live read-only bindings: assigning to one throws TypeError, but mutating an imported object's properties is fine
The module specifier must be a string literal — nothing between import and from can be dynamic
Debug starter: importing a default-only module with braces { X } yields a missing-export error or undefined — check what's actually exported

chapters.title: Internals: How the Engine Runs a Module Graph
points: ESM runs in three phases: parse (build graph, find imports) → instantiate/link (wire bindings) → evaluate (run bodies)
CJS conflates the phases: each require() resolves, loads, and runs inline during evaluation — that's why it can be dynamic
Parse-time safety: missing exports and most syntax errors throw before a single line of your code runs
Evaluation order: depth-first, dependencies before dependents (post-order traversal of the graph)
Exports are live bindings to variables, not snapshots: importers observe changes to an exported let
Canonical example: export let count = 0; export function inc() { count++ } — importers see the updated count without re-importing
Imports behave like const: reassignment throws, but mutating properties of an imported object is allowed
Implicit strict mode plus top-level this === undefined in every module — silent behavior change when converting scripts
TDZ across modules: touching an imported let/const before its declaration evaluates → 'Cannot access x before initialization' (key to cycles, ch. 6)
Top-level await (ES2022): a module with TLA evaluates like an async function body — importers wait for it to finish
Node's module map guarantees single evaluation even with concurrent and dynamic loads
Rule: hoisted function declarations survive early calls across the graph; touching imported let/const early does not

chapters.title: Circular Imports: Cycles Done Right(ish)
points: Cycle anatomy: A imports B imports A — common with parent↔child components, factories, and shared-constant files
CJS behavior: when B requires A mid-evaluation, it receives A's partial exports object — whatever was assigned so far
CJS symptom: values destructured from that partial object are undefined copies; reading a.helper after A finishes works
CJS deeper trap: if A later does module.exports = {...} (reassignment), B still holds the stale first object reference
ESM behavior: hoisted function declarations survive cycles — the binding exists at link time, the body runs later
ESM failure mode: module-level code touching B's const/let while it's still in the TDZ → ReferenceError at evaluation
'Cannot access X before initialization' in production = a cycle problem until proven otherwise — trace the import chain
Fix #1: move the shared thing into a third module that both sides import — break the cycle structurally
Fix #2: defer access — call imported functions inside handlers/callbacks instead of at module top level
Detection tooling: madge --circular, dpdm, ESLint rule import/no-cycle — wire into CI before cycles wire themselves in
Judgment call: function-only cycles often work but still couple modules and break tree shaking and bundler edge cases — refactor anyway

chapters.title: Dynamic import(): Loading on Demand
points: import(specifier) is a runtime operator returning a Promise of the module namespace — the specifier string can be built dynamically
Legal anywhere an expression is: inside if, event handlers, setTimeout, loops — static import cannot say this
Killer use case — code splitting: const mod = await import('./heavy-chart.js') splits it into a lazily fetched chunk
Failure is a rejected promise: wrap in try/catch and render a fallback when the chunk fails to load
Shape note: dynamically importing a CJS module puts its exports under .default — prefer const mod = await import(...), then mod.default
Dynamic import works inside CJS files in modern Node — it's the supported way to load ESM from CJS, since require() couldn't
Webpack hints: /* webpackChunkName: "chart" */ names the chunk; prefetch/preload magic comments tune when the browser fetches it
Bundler-specific tuning: Rollup/Vite manualChunks and esbuild splitting decide where dynamic chunks land — import() alone doesn't
Interaction with top-level await: awaiting import() at a module's top level stalls every importer — do it inside functions
Not free: each dynamic chunk is a network round trip — split features, not every file; measure first-paint impact
import.meta.resolve(specifier) resolves to a URL without loading — useful for workers and prefetch planning
Rule of thumb: static import for the critical path; dynamic import for routes, modals, editors, charts, i18n locales, polyfills

chapters.title: Bundler Semantics: Tree Shaking to Chunks
points: What a bundler does: parse each module to an AST, build the import graph, wrap and concatenate with a mini runtime, emit optimized bundles
Static imports make the graph knowable at build time — the entire reason ESM optimizes better than CJS
Tree shaking: follow named imports, mark unused exports dead, let the minifier strip them — mark-and-sweep over the module graph
Tree shaking only works on declarative ESM syntax — require() calls and computed property access defeat it
Side effects kill shaking: top-level polyfills, CSS imports, or patched globals force bundlers to keep whole modules
Declare cleanliness: "sideEffects": false (or a file list) in package.json unlocks aggressive shaking for libraries
Scope hoisting (Rollup's signature move): merge modules into one scope, eliminating per-module wrappers for smaller, faster output
Dynamic import becomes a chunk boundary: bundlers cut the graph at import() and emit each specifier as a lazily fetched file
CJS interop inside bundles: the __esModule flag plus interop helpers synthesize a default so mixed graphs keep working
HTTP/2 multiplexing didn't remove bundling: thousands of tiny files still pay request, parse, and compression overhead
Bundlers differ: Rollup and esbuild shake more aggressively by default; webpack needs production mode plus sideEffects hints
Native alternative: import maps alias bare specifiers directly in the browser — great for prototypes, but no minification or shaking

chapters.title: Interop & Packaging: ESM + CJS in the Wild
points: Node's extension rules: .mjs is always ESM, .cjs always CJS, plain .js follows the nearest package.json "type" field
"type": "module" flips defaults repo-wide — and can break tooling that require()s your .js configs; rename those to .cjs
"exports" field: defines public entry points, blocks deep imports, and selects files per condition — import / require / node / browser
Field soup decoded: "main" (legacy CJS), "module" (bundler-only ESM hint, ignored by Node), "exports" (the modern source of truth)
Dual package hazard: shipping both formats means apps can load two copies — split state, broken instanceof; solve with one entry plus conditions
ESM importing CJS: module.exports lands on default; Node's cjs-module-lexer guesses named exports — safest is default or namespace access
CJS importing ESM: the classic answer is await import(); newer Node adds require(esm) with constraints — no top-level await in the ESM
No __dirname/__filename in ESM: rebuild them with dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))
Browser loading: <script type="module"> is deferred by default, strict-mode, and requires CORS — imports fail from file://
Top-level await is a compatibility boundary: a module with TLA can't be require()d or bundled down to CJS targets
Test-runner transforms (Jest's CJS transform, Vitest) can mask real semantics — live bindings and TDZ errors may behave differently under test
Migration playbook: flip type, add extensions, replace __dirname, publish via conditions, keep a CJS escape hatch for config files

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & The Closing Map
points: Mistake: exports = { ... } in CJS silently exports nothing — the alias detached; always use module.exports
Mistake: omitting extensions in Node ESM ('./utils') → ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, even though require() tolerated it
Mistake: conditional static imports — SyntaxError; anything runtime-dependent must use dynamic import()
Mistake: braces on a default-only export or no braces on a named export — check the module's actual export shape first
Mistake: assigning to an imported binding → 'Assignment to constant variable'; export an explicit setter function instead
Mistake: assuming imports are snapshots — a later read of a live let binding can diverge from what you logged earlier
Mistake: barrels that also import side-effectful CSS or polyfills — tree shaking keeps them anyway; keep barrels pure re-exports
Mistake: top-level await in a widely shared module silently serializes every importer's startup
Error triage order: SyntaxError at parse → missing-export or TDZ ReferenceError at link/evaluate → runtime errors after; the phase names the bug class
Choosing today: app code on modern Node → ESM everywhere; publishing a library → ESM-first with conditions, or a dual build
Architecture defaults: static imports for the critical path, dynamic import() for heavy or rare features, zero unintentional cycles
One-line summary: CJS = dynamic, synchronous, value snapshots at require time; ESM = static, async-capable, live-bound graph — and every modern tool assumes the latter
